Cf. also : a tamou I was eating, a tamou I eat ( from something), a tamou I was eating ( from something) The following appear to be distinguished by stress : 1) béràn body, hair, búran adulteress barons large turtle, baron poor ( ' marked over stressed syllable) But stress and tone are interwoven to a large extent, and their interrelationship is still far from clear . new_statements.rule_in_words: Nyimang/Ama is a three-level tone language (Stevenson 1957; Tucker & Bryan 1966; confirmed by Norton 2020 from modern fieldwork). Stevenson additionally reports that stress is lexically distinctive: he gives word pairs distinguished by stress alone (béràn 'body, hair' vs búran 'adulteress'; barons 'large turtle' vs baron 'poor'), so stress position is not stated as rule-governed (initial in the first pair, contrasting with a shifted stress in the second), and he explicitly says the stress-tone relation is unresolved, suggesting tonal forms have been 'overlaid with stress patterns'. Tucker & Bryan 1966 §2b repeat this as 'Stress also appears to distinguish words' but leave stress unmarked elsewhere; Ruhlen 1975 codes the language as 'phonemic stress'; Hyman 1977 lists it among languages whose stress placement could not be classified. Sub-reading for position: lexical (unpredictable).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any accessed source.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; Stevenson himself flags the analysis as provisional ('interrelationship is still far from clear'). Norton 2020, the only modern first-hand description opened, describes three level tones and says nothing about stress at all.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, isolated lexical items (minimal pairs in citation form). Snippet-only access: the primary text was not opened in full and the page number is unrecovered; the second-hand form of the same claim ('phonemic stress') is fully opened and saved in Ruhlen 1975 p. 250 (PDF page 266).
new_statements.identity_note: Nyimang = Ama [nyi], amas1236 (self-name ámá; 'Nyimang'/'Nyima' in Stevenson, Tucker & Bryan, Ruhlen, Hyman). Stevenson's and Tucker & Bryan's Nyimang sections treat Nyimang proper (Ama) with Afitti/Dinik [aft, afit1238] contrasted inside the same sketch; the statement quoted is explicitly about NYIMANG. de Voogt 2009 ('a tone language with stress', two tones) describes Afitti only and must not be transferred to Ama. Norton 2020 is Ama proper (villages west/north-west of Dilling).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Nyimang has three level tones (contour tones only from reduced disyllables), lexical and grammatical tone, and in addition stress 'appears to distinguish words': the pairs body/adulteress and large turtle/poor differ by which syllable is stressed (initial vs. non-initial, as far as the scanned shows). new_statements.identity_note: All three works are about Nyimang = Ama [nyi] (glottocode amas1236). Tucker & Bryan treat Nyimang and Afitti together in one chapter but state 'All examples are from NYIMANG, unless otherwise stated'; the quoted §2 examples are Nyimang. Norton 2012 describes Ama and notes that some example speakers are from Tundia in the western part of the Ama area.
